Class WhoStatelessConfigurer

java.lang.Object
org.springframework.security.config.annotation.SecurityConfigurerAdapter<org.springframework.security.web.DefaultSecurityFilterChain, org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity>
org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.configurers.AbstractHttpConfigurer<WhoStatelessConfigurer, org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity>
org.jwcarman.who.spring.security.WhoStatelessConfigurer
All Implemented Interfaces:
org.springframework.security.config.annotation.SecurityConfigurer<org.springframework.security.web.DefaultSecurityFilterChain, org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity>
public final class WhoStatelessConfigurer extends org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.configurers.AbstractHttpConfigurer<WhoStatelessConfigurer, org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity>
Mounts who's stateless sign-in methods, every StatelessLoginMethod bean (API keys, bearer JWTs), into a chain that never reads or creates a session:
  • the security context lives in the request only, and the request's session is hidden from the whole chain, so a session cookie that another chain made signs nothing in here, and is neither given a new id nor ended. Application code on this chain cannot use a session either: asking for one (HttpSession parameters, @SessionAttributes, session-scoped beans, flash attributes) fails with IllegalStateException;
  • logout is not mounted: there is no session to end;
  • CSRF protection is off, because nothing on this chain rides along with a request by itself: a forged cross-site request cannot attach the header a credential travels in. That holds only while the application adds no credential a browser sends by itself to this chain, such as httpBasic() or client certificates. An application's own csrf(...) settings for this chain are replaced;
  • a signed-out request gets 401, with a WWW-Authenticate header for each method that has a scheme (StatelessLoginMethod.challenge()), and a denied one 403, both handed to the application's exception handling.

After the sign-in methods it applies every StatelessEndpoints bean, such as the caller's API keys under /who/me/api-keys.

It mounts no browser sign-in method, even when one is on the classpath, so an application can give its API a chain of its own beside a browser chain. With no stateless method in the application, building the chain fails; so does a chain whose sessions are turned back on after this configurer, with sessionManagement(...) or securityContext(...), since it would then sign requests in from a session with CSRF off. Obtain one with WhoSecurity.stateless().
